nameStory: The snowy urola moth gets its name from its pristine white appearance that resembles fresh snow against a windowpane. The genus name 'Urola' comes from Greek roots, while 'nivalis' means 'of the snow' in Latin, perfectly capturing this little moth's clean, wintry look.
description: The snowy urola moth is a small, delicate member of the crambid snout moth family that looks like a tiny piece of white paper with wings. These moths have a wingspan of just over half an inch to nearly an inch across, making them quite petite compared to the larger moths you might see at your porch light. Their wings are predominantly white with subtle markings, and like other snout moths, they have noticeable forward-projecting mouthparts that give them a distinctive profile. You'll typically spot them from late spring through early fall as they go through two generations each year.

idTips.label: Wing color and pattern
idTips.description: Pure white wings with subtle gray or brownish markings along the edges and sometimes faint lines across the forewings that feel papery-thin to the touch

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small wingspan of 15-23mm (about the size of your thumbnail), making them noticeably smaller than most other white moths you'll encounter

idTips.label: Snout projection
idTips.description: Distinctive forward-pointing mouthparts that stick out like a tiny beak when viewed from the side, characteristic of all snout moths

idTips.label: Body shape
idTips.description: Slender, elongated body that's white to pale gray, often held at an angle when resting with wings folded tent-like over the back

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Weak, fluttering flight that seems almost ghostly as they drift around grassy areas and landscape plantings in the evening

habitat: Look for snowy urola moths in suburban yards, parks, and gardens where ornamental shrubs like privet are planted, as well as in grassy fields and meadow edges. They're particularly common around landscaped areas with a mix of lawn grasses and ornamental plantings. You'll often find them near outdoor lights at night or resting on vegetation during the day in areas with good grass cover.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late May, with the first generation appearing as a fresh wave of pristine white moths around grassy areas and gardens.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs during summer months when both generations may overlap, making this the best time to observe adults flying around lights or resting on vegetation during the day.
seasonality.fall: The second generation is active through early fall, with adults becoming less common as temperatures drop and they complete their breeding cycle.
seasonality.winter: Adults are absent during winter months, with the species likely overwintering as larvae feeding on grass roots and stems beneath the snow.

funFact: Despite their innocent snowy appearance, these moths are actually garden troublemakers—their caterpillars are considered pests of privet hedges, the same ornamental shrubs that homeowners spend hundreds of dollars maintaining for privacy fencing!
confusionNotes: Snowy urola moths can be confused with other small white moths, but their tiny size and distinctive snout immediately separate them from larger white species. Remember: if it's small, white, and has a beak-like projection, you've found your snowy urola!
contextualKnowledge: The name 'snout moth' refers to the extended labial palps (mouthparts) that project forward like a snout, which is a defining characteristic of the entire Crambidae family—it's not that they actually have mammal-like snouts, but rather modified feeding structures.
compareHints: Since the snowy urola moth is the only Urola species in New England, compare it to other small white crambid moths in the region. It's distinguished from similar species by its particularly clean white coloration with minimal markings and its relatively small size. Most other white snout moths in the area tend to be either larger or have more distinct gray or brown patterning on their wings.
